claim: On an 8x A100 NVLink 3.0 node the authors' multi-GPU SGEMM reaches >80% of peak for 3-8 GPUs at tile size 1024 (N=90000), with strong scaling close to ideal.
stance_target: NVLink-connected server GPUs scale multi-GPU GEMM near-ideally
quoted_support: For all NGP Us = 3–8 we see the optimum Ni = 1024. At this tile size the eﬃciency of the algorithm (attained FLOPS over theoretical peak performance) reaches more than 80% for all NGP Us.

claim: On a 4x AMD RX 6900 XT node connected by PCIe 4.0, the same algorithm's efficiency falls below 40% for 3 and 4 GPUs.
stance_target: PCIe-attached consumer GPUs lose most of their multi-GPU GEMM efficiency
quoted_support: The results show surprisingly modest performance and low eﬃciency that is lower than 40% for 3 and for 4 GPUs.

claim: A single-GPU SGEMM launch on RX 6900 XT reaches only 8 TFLOPS of the 22.5 TFLOPS peak, with 'considerable delays between data transfers'.
stance_target: consumer GPUs struggle to overlap computation with data transfer
scope_conditions: RX 6900 XT, single-GPU SGEMM, N=32768, tile 8192
quoted_support: the performance is 8 TFLOPS from the peak 22.5 TFLOPS. Figure 6 shows also considerable delays between data transfers.

claim: The authors conclude the multi-GPU performance of their algorithm 'can not be transferred easily to the consumer-grade GPU systems' because consumer GPUs are not built to compute and transfer simultaneously.
stance_target: consumer/mining-class GPUs are a poor substrate for communication-heavy multi-GPU work
quoted_support: We suppose that these problems might be explained by the diﬃculty for the GPU (that is a consumer GPU, not a server grade GPU) to perform computations and data transfers simultaneously. This observation points to the fact that the multi-GPU performance of the algorithm considered can not be transferred easily to the consumer-grade GPU systems.

claim: Table 1 platform parameters: A100 peak FP32 19.5 TFLOPS (real 18.4), FP32 tensor-core peak 156 TFLOPS (real 124), peak GPU-GPU 300 GB/s (real 281); RX 6900 XT peak FP32 22.5 TFLOPS (real 21.4), peak GPU-GPU 32 GB/s (real 25.5).
stance_target: reference hardware parameters for NVLink vs PCIe multi-GPU nodes
quoted_support: Peak GPU-GPU bandwidth (GB/s) 300 32 / Real GPU-GPU bandwidth (GB/s) 281 25.5

claim: Turning tensor cores on raises absolute TFLOPS but drops efficiency below 40% at 8 GPUs, i.e. tensor-core throughput does not rescue multi-GPU scaling.
stance_target: tensor cores fix multi-GPU scaling inefficiency
quoted_support: Despite signiﬁcant acceleration in absolute values, the level of eﬃciency with tensor cores becomes lower (even lower than 40% N = 8).

claim: The algorithm beats cuBLAS-XT on the same 8x A100 problem (N=90000), showing library-level multi-GPU GEMM leaves performance on the table.
stance_target: hand-tuned multi-GPU GEMM can outperform vendor libraries
quoted_support: Figure 2c shows the performance of cuBlas-XT for the exactly same problem (N = 90000, the points correspond to the minimum execution times at the variation of the tile size). One can see that the performance of cuBlas-XT is signiﬁcantly worse that the performance of our algorithm.

claim: The PCIe 4.0 testbed delivers 32 GB/s peak / 25.5 GB/s real GPU-GPU bandwidth, roughly 25-32x the CMP box's Gen2 x4 link, so the consumer-GPU penalty observed here should be at least as severe on the CMP box.
stance_target: transferability of the PCIe consumer-GPU penalty to a Gen2 x4 CMP 170HX box
scope_conditions: PCIe 4.0 x16 vs PCIe Gen2 x4
quoted_support: The second platform is the server with 4 AMD RX 6900 XT GPUs connected by PCIe 4.0

claim: The RX 6900 XT result is anomalous relative to older consumer cards: a GTX1070 benchmark of the same algorithm showed efficiency over 50%, so the PCIe penalty is not purely a function of link bandwidth.
stance_target: whether the consumer-GPU penalty is monotonic in link bandwidth
scope_conditions: RX 6900 XT vs GTX1070, same algorithm
quoted_support: It is a strange fact since even for the quite old Nvidia GTX1070 GPUs the similar benchmark showed eﬃciency over 50% (see [6]).
